To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) people blame robots more than humans for inaction than for action in a moral decision-making dilemma, (2) this HR asymmetry in blame for inaction and action is present only when the robot appears as a mechanical-looking robot but not a humanoid robot, and (3) this HR asymmetries in blame for inacton and action is present for both a moral and an immoral dilemma.

(1) people blame robots more than humans for inaction in a moral dilemma and blame humans more than robots for action in a moral dilemmas (HR asymmetry); and (2) this asymmetry is present when the robot is depicted as a mechanical robot but not when it is depicted as a humanoid robot.

(a) the appearance of the robot influences moral judgments about the robot, (b) the appearance of a robot is more influential in moral judgments than the robot's action, and (c) the appearance of an action influences moral judgments about a robot, but only when the robot's appearance does not influence moral judgments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how robots and humans are perceived in moral dilemmas.
how people make moral judgments about robots, which robots are seen as moral and immoral, and how robot appearance affects people’s moral judgments.
the question of how people evaluate robots that make moral decisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
people's judgments about robots are influenced by their representations of robots, and that these representations are not necessarily the same across different robot designs.
people blame robots (and human-like robots) more for inaction in a moral dilemma than for action.
people are more forgiving of a robot than of a human for failing to save four people, but only when the robot appears to be a mechanical robot, not a humanlike one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
when people judge robots, the robot's appearance affects the way they judge its morality.

the HR asymmetry appears when a robot looks like a mechanical robot and not a humanoid robot, but when a robot looks human-like, the HR asymmetry disappears and people's judgments are more similar to those made about a human.
people's moral judgments of robots are influenced by their representation of the robot and that this representation is affected by the robot's appearance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people's moral judgments of robots are not as simple as one might think.
the HR asymmetry is not an artifact of the robot's verbal description, as some have claimed, but rather a reflection of the fact that people do not see robots as fully human.
people's moral judgments depend on the robot they are thinking of.
